# The Shape of a Secret: Why Four Beautiful Ideas Fail to Factor a Number

Take two large prime numbers, multiply them together, and publish the answer. That single act — trivial to perform, apparently impossible to undo — is the hinge on which a great deal of modern cryptography turns. The number $N = pq$ is public; the primes $p$ and $q$ are the secret. Everyone can check that $N$ is what it claims to be. Almost nobody can pull it apart.

What makes this asymmetry so strange is that $N$ is *not* hiding its factors in any obvious way. They are right there, in a hundred different disguises. The number $N$ knows how many units it has. It knows which residues are squares. It knows the shape of its own multiplication table. Every one of those facts is, in principle, entangled with $p$ and $q$. So why can't we just *ask*?

This article is about four serious attempts to ask — four different mathematical objects attached to $N$, each of which genuinely does contain the factorization, and each of which, on close inspection, refuses to hand it over. The failures are not embarrassments. They are theorems. And together they trace out a surprisingly crisp boundary: a precise description of *why* the information is present but unreachable.

---

## The setup: a number and its shadow

Fix two distinct primes $p$ and $q$ and set $N = pq$. The world we work in is the ring of integers modulo $N$, written $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$: the numbers $0, 1, \dots, N-1$ with addition and multiplication wrapped around at $N$.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem this ring is secretly a *pair* of rings glued together:
$$\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}.$$
Every residue $a$ mod $N$ is really a pair — its shadow mod $p$ and its shadow mod $q$ — and every arithmetic operation acts on the two shadows independently. Somebody who knows $p$ and $q$ can see both shadows. Somebody who knows only $N$ sees only the glued object, never the seam.

Almost everything below is a story about trying to find the seam.

---

## Attempt 1: Ask the squares

Here is a very natural probe. For a prime $p$ and a number $a$ not divisible by $p$, the *Legendre symbol* $(a \mid p)$ is $+1$ if $a$ is a perfect square modulo $p$ and $-1$ if it is not. Exactly half the nonzero residues mod $p$ are squares, so this symbol is a perfectly balanced coin — but a coin whose flips are determined by arithmetic, not chance.

Now, for our composite $N = pq$, each unit $a$ has *two* Legendre symbols, one for each shadow: $(a \mid p)$ and $(a \mid q)$. Individually these are pure gold — knowing $(a \mid p)$ for a few $a$'s is knowing something genuinely about $p$. But we can't compute them, because computing them requires knowing $p$.

What we *can* compute from $N$ alone is their product, the Jacobi symbol $J(a \mid N) = (a\mid p)(a \mid q)$. That is a classical, fast computation — a cousin of the Euclidean algorithm.

So here is the tempting move. Consider the set of residues where the two hidden symbols *agree*:
$$A(N) \;=\; \{\, a \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times \;:\; (a\mid p) = (a\mid q) \,\}.$$

Why is this attractive? Because it is *symmetric in exactly the right way*. Any genuine handle on the factorization must eventually break the symmetry between $p$ and $q$ — but many natural quantities do not, and those get discarded early. The agreement set survives that first filter: it is unchanged if you swap the roles of $p$ and $q$, and unchanged under the natural conjugation symmetry of the ring. It is a bona fide invariant of the *unordered* pair $\{p, q\}$. And its definition mentions $p$ and $q$ explicitly, so surely its size should depend on them?

It does not. Here is the first theorem.

> **The Agreement Collapse.** Let $p$ be an odd prime and $q \ne p$ a prime, $N = pq$. Then the agreement set has exactly
> $$|A(N)| \;=\; \frac{\varphi(N)}{2} \;=\; \frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2}$$
> elements, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function. Moreover $A(N)$ is precisely the set of $a$ with $J(a \mid N) = +1$.

The proof is a single elegant move, and it is worth seeing because it explains *why* the collapse is inevitable. Using the Chinese Remainder Theorem, choose a unit $u$ that is a non-square modulo $p$ but is congruent to $1$ modulo $q$. Such a $u$ exists for any odd $p$: pick any non-residue mod $p$, pick $1$ mod $q$, and glue. Now multiply. Since Legendre symbols are multiplicative, $(au \mid p) = -(a\mid p)$ while $(au\mid q) = (a \mid q)$. In other words, multiplying by $u$ flips one symbol and leaves the other alone — so it converts agreement into disagreement and back. Multiplication by $u$ is a bijection of the units, so it puts the agreement set into perfect one-to-one correspondence with its complement. Two equal halves. Exactly $\varphi(N)/2$.

And the second half of the theorem is even more deflating: agreement $(a\mid p) = (a\mid q)$ happens if and only if the product $(a\mid p)(a\mid q)$ equals $+1$ — because both factors are $\pm 1$. But that product *is* the Jacobi symbol, computable from $N$ without knowing anything. The set we thought was a secret window is just the level set of a public function.

This is character orthogonality doing what it always does: an aggregate built from characters that is invariant under all the available symmetries is forced to be a function of the ambient modulus alone. The count $\varphi(N)/2$ knows $\varphi(N)$ — and knowing $\varphi(N)$ is already equivalent to knowing the factorization. The window is a mirror.

---

## Attempt 2: Ask the shape

If numeric probes collapse, try a *shape*. Build a graph.

The **zero-divisor graph** of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ has as vertices all the residues $0 < x < N$ that share a factor with $N$, with an edge between $x \ne y$ whenever $xy \equiv 0 \pmod N$. This is a purely combinatorial object — no numbers designated as "the answer", just dots and lines.

For $N = pq$ the picture is startlingly clean, and completely determined.

> **The Zero-Divisor Graph of a Semiprime.** Let $p \ne q$ be primes and $N = pq$. Then the nonzero zero-divisors split into two *wings*: the nonzero multiples of $p$ below $N$, of which there are $q - 1$, and the nonzero multiples of $q$, of which there are $p - 1$. The wings are disjoint and exhaust the vertex set, so the graph has
> $$|V| = (p-1) + (q-1) = p + q - 2$$
> vertices. Two vertices are adjacent **if and only if** they lie in *different* wings. That is, the graph is the complete bipartite graph $K_{q-1,\,p-1}$.

Each direction of the adjacency statement is a one-line argument. If $x = pa$ and $y = qb$ then $xy = pq\,ab$ is a multiple of $N$: every cross-wing pair is an edge. Conversely if $x$ and $y$ are both multiples of $p$ and $N = pq$ divides $xy$, then in particular $q$ divides $xy$, so $q$ divides one of them — but that residue would then be divisible by both $p$ and $q$, hence by $N$, hence be $0$ or at least $N$; contradiction. So there are no edges inside a wing.

The consequences are immediate and, for a would-be factorer, tantalizing. Every vertex in the $p$-wing has exactly $p - 1$ neighbours (the whole $q$-wing) and every vertex in the $q$-wing has exactly $q - 1$. So:

> **Factor Recovery from Degrees.** For any vertex $x$ of the graph, $\deg(x) + 1$ is a prime factor of $N$.

You do not need the whole graph. You need one vertex and its degree. The factorization is written on the face of every single node.

Here is where the trap closes. Suppose you have a vertex $x$. By definition a vertex is a residue $0 < x < N$ that is *not* coprime to $N$. So $\gcd(x, N)$ is a nontrivial divisor: it is $p$ or $q$.

> **The Circularity.** Exhibiting a single vertex of the zero-divisor graph already exhibits a factor of $N$, via one greatest-common-divisor computation.

The graph does determine $\{p,q\}$ — that is a theorem, not a heuristic. But the vertex set *is* the divisor structure. To draw the graph you must first find its dots, and finding a dot is already winning. In a haystack of $N$ residues there are only $p + q - 2$ dots; finding one by search is trial division wearing a new hat.

This is the sharpest and most instructive of the four closures, because it shows that the failure is not a failure of information. It is a failure of *access*. The structural witness exists; it is simply not cheaper than the thing it witnesses.

There is a further twist. What does the graph actually tell you, as a number? Its vertex count is $p + q - 2$. Add two and you have the *trace* $s = p+q$; together with the *norm* $N = pq$ you get the quadratic
$$X^2 - sX + N = 0,$$
whose two roots are exactly $p$ and $q$. So the combinatorial object, for all its apparent novelty, delivers precisely the same numeric datum — the sum of the primes — that every other successful line of attack delivers. The shape collapses onto the number.

---

## Attempt 3: Ask a random residue — and then ask cleverly

How likely is a blind guess to work? Pick $a$ uniformly at random from $1, \dots, N-1$ and compute $\gcd(a, N)$. You succeed exactly when $a$ is a vertex of the graph above, so your success probability is
$$\frac{p+q-2}{N}.$$

> **The Atomic Uniform Bound.** If $p \le q$, a single uniform query succeeds with probability at most $2/p$.

And how small can that be? By the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, $(p+q)^2 \ge 4pq = 4N$, with equality only when $p = q$. So the success probability is roughly $2/\sqrt{N}$ at best, when the two primes are balanced — which is exactly how cryptographic moduli are chosen. This is the **noise floor**: a random shot in the dark hits with probability about $N^{-1/2}$, and no amount of cleverness in *choosing the distribution* fixes it, because the target set has only $p + q - 2$ members out of $N$.

Now here is the refinement that this round produced, and it matters.

Consider Pollard's rho walk: start at some $x_0$ and iterate $x \mapsto x^2 + 1 \pmod N$. Measure the *density* of factor-bearing information in the resulting sample set. It is enormously higher than $N^{-1/2}$ — in experiments, essentially $1$. Does that break the noise floor?

No — and the reason is precise. The walk's samples are not independent draws; they are *correlated*, and the correlation is exactly the point.

> **Reduction-Compatibility.** The map $x \mapsto x^2+1$ commutes with reduction modulo any $m$: if $a \equiv b \pmod m$ then $a^2+1 \equiv b^2+1 \pmod m$, and hence all iterates stay congruent. So the walk modulo $N$ *covers* a walk modulo $p$.

> **Guaranteed Collision.** The walk modulo $p$ lives in a set of only $p$ states, so among the first $p+1$ iterates two must coincide modulo $p$. That is pigeonhole, not probability: there exist $i < j \le p$ with $p \mid x_j - x_i$.

> **Extraction.** If a prime $p$ divides $d$ and $q$ does not, then $\gcd(d, pq) = p$ exactly. So any collision mod $p$ that is not simultaneously a collision mod $q$ hands over the factor.

Those three statements, stitched together, are the correctness core of Pollard's rho method — with no randomness hypothesis at all. The density really is high. So why is factoring still hard?

Because of the *aggregation price*. A collision is a statement about a **pair** of samples. To find the pair you must compare them, and comparing all pairs among $T$ samples costs $\binom{T}{2}$ operations. With the pigeonhole guarantee $T = p+1$, that is
$$\binom{p+1}{2} \;\ge\; p,$$
already more than the $p$ trial divisions you were trying to avoid. The unconditional density gain is real and it is paid for in full at the checkout. (The famous $\sqrt{p}$ running time of rho comes not from this unconditional argument but from a birthday-paradox heuristic plus Floyd's cycle-finding trick that avoids explicit pairwise comparison — a known method, not a new escape.)

The lesson is a scoping lesson, and it is the intellectual centre of this whole round: **the noise floor bounds atomic, uniform primitives — a single query drawn from a distribution close to uniform — and it is not a density theorem about correlated or derived samples.** Correlated samples can be dense. They just cost more to read.

---

## Attempt 4: Ask the digits

The last attempt is the most geometric. Write $N$, $p$, and $q$ in base $b$. Multiplication of $p$ and $q$ is a *convolution* of their digit sequences, plus carries. If we introduce a variable $w_{ij} = p_i q_j$ for each pair of digit positions, the digit equations become **linear** in the $w_{ij}$ — and linear equations over the integers define a lattice, where the celebrated LLL algorithm finds short vectors fast. Is the factorization the short vector?

Consider the smallest nontrivial case: two digits each. Write the digit functional
$$\Phi_b(w) \;=\; \sum_{i,j} w_{ij}\, b^{\,i+j},$$
and for digit vectors $u = (u_0,u_1)$, $v=(v_0,v_1)$ write $\langle u \rangle_b = u_0 + u_1 b$ for the number they encode.

> **Faithfulness.** For the rank-one matrix $w = u \otimes v$ (that is, $w_{ij} = u_i v_j$), we have $\Phi_b(u\otimes v) = \langle u\rangle_b \cdot \langle v\rangle_b$. So genuine factorizations of $N$ are exactly the *rank-one* solutions of $\Phi_b(w) = N$.

> **The Discarded Constraint.** A $2\times 2$ matrix is rank one exactly when its determinant vanishes. The determinant is quadratic; the relaxation is linear; so the relaxation cannot see it.

That is not yet fatal — perhaps rank-one solutions happen to be the *shortest* ones. They do not, and here is the reason, which is a single explicit matrix.

> **The Carry Commutator.** Let $C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $\Phi_b(C) = b^{0+1} - b^{1+0} = 0$ for **every** base $b$. Its squared Frobenius norm is $2$ — a constant, independent of $N$.

The matrix $C$ is invisible to the digit functional because the coefficient $b^{i+j}$ depends only on $i+j$, so the linearization cannot distinguish position $(0,1)$ from position $(1,0)$. That degeneracy is precisely the carry information the relaxation threw away. And it is devastating:

> **Non-Isolation.** For every factorization target $u \otimes v$ there is a matrix $w$ with the *same* digit value $\Phi_b(w) = N$, with **nonzero determinant** — hence not a factorization — at squared distance at most $8$ from the target, no matter how large $N$ is.

The construction is a two-line case split: perturb by $C$ or by $2C$. The determinant of $u\otimes v + cC$ is $c(u_0v_1 - u_1v_0) + c^2$, which is a nonzero number for $c = 1$ or for $c = 2$ (both fail only if a single integer is simultaneously $-1$ and $-2$). The perturbation has squared norm $2c^2 \le 8$.

Meanwhile the target itself has squared norm $(u_0^2+u_1^2)(v_0^2+v_1^2)$, which grows with the digits of $p$ and $q$. So the true answer sits inside an $O(1)$-radius cloud of impostors, in a lattice whose typical short vectors are of comparable length — exactly the "target at the Gaussian heuristic" phenomenon the experiments measured. Lattice reduction dutifully returns *a* short vector. There is no reason on earth for it to be the right one.

---

## What the four failures add up to

Four probes: an arithmetic aggregate, a combinatorial shape, a dynamical sampler, a geometric relaxation. Each genuinely contains the factorization. Each is closed, and each is closed for a *different* reason:

1. **The aggregate collapses.** Symmetry is a double-edged sword: an invariant symmetric enough to be well-defined without knowing $p$ and $q$ is symmetric enough to be computable without them. $|A(N)| = \varphi(N)/2$; the set is the Jacobi level set.
2. **The shape is circular.** The zero-divisor graph is exactly $K_{q-1,p-1}$ and its degrees give the factors — but its vertices *are* the factors' multiples, so drawing it presupposes the answer.
3. **The sampler is dense but expensive.** Correlated samples beat the noise floor honestly; the floor was only ever a bound on atomic uniform queries. What they cannot beat is the quadratic cost of the pairwise aggregation needed to cash the density in.
4. **The relaxation is degenerate.** Linearizing the digits creates an explicit constant-norm kernel vector, so the target is never isolated among short vectors.

There is a pleasing final image. Take logarithms of the divisor equation $xy = N$: it becomes $X + Y = \log N$, a straight line. In the min-plus (tropical) world, where "addition" is taking the minimum and "multiplication" is ordinary addition, that line has a corner sitting exactly at $\tfrac{1}{2}\log N$ — the location of $\sqrt N$. Every factor pair of $N$ straddles that corner: if $p \le q$ then $p^2 \le N \le q^2$. The corner is the noise floor made geometric. Every one of the four attempts above was, in its own language, an attempt to walk around the corner rather than through it. None of them made it.

That is not a proof that factoring is hard. Nobody has one, and nobody is close. But it is something valuable and rarer than it sounds: a set of theorems that says exactly *which* good ideas do not work, and exactly *why*. In a field where the space of plausible-sounding attacks is enormous, a precisely-scoped negative result is a map. It tells the next explorer where the cliffs are — and, by elimination, where the unexplored ground still lies.

# Hypothesis Closures for Semiprime Structure: Character Aggregates, Zero-Divisor Graphs, Correlated Samplers, and Digit Lattices

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-08-13

---

## Abstract

We give a rigorous, self-contained treatment of four structural probes of a semiprime $N = pq$ ($p \ne q$ prime), each of which was proposed as a route to a factor-revealing witness lying outside the known classification of numeric witnesses, and we close all four.

First, we study the **agreement set** $A(N) = \{a \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times : (a\mid p) = (a\mid q)\}$, an aggregate invariant under both the swap $p \leftrightarrow q$ and conjugation. We prove that $2|A(N)| = \varphi(N)$ exactly (for odd $p$), and that $A(N)$ coincides with the level set $\{a : J(a\mid N) = 1\}$ of the Jacobi symbol, an $N$-computable function. The aggregate therefore collapses onto the quadratic character modulo $N$ and carries no information beyond $\varphi(N)$.

Second, we determine the **zero-divisor graph** $\Gamma(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ completely: its vertex set splits into two wings of sizes $q-1$ and $p-1$, adjacency holds exactly across wings, so $\Gamma \cong K_{q-1,\,p-1}$; consequently $|V| = p + q - 2$ and $\deg(x) + 1$ is a prime factor of $N$ for every vertex $x$. We show that this structural witness collapses onto the numeric trace witness ($p$ and $q$ are the roots of $X^2 - (|V|+2)X + N$) and that it is circular: exhibiting one vertex already exhibits a factor, since $\gcd(x, N) \in \{p,q\}$.

Third, we prove a **noise-floor bound for atomic uniform primitives**: a single uniform query on $[1,N)$ reveals a factor with probability $(p+q-2)/N \le 2/p$, and $(p+q)^2 \ge 4N$ with equality iff $p = q$, so the floor is $\approx 2/\sqrt N$ for balanced semiprimes. We contrast this with the *correlated* sample set generated by the static rho map $x \mapsto x^2+1$, for which we prove unconditionally — by reduction-compatibility plus pigeonhole — that a factor-bearing pair exists among the first $p+1$ iterates. The density gain is real; we prove it is paid for by the aggregation cost $\binom{p+1}{2} \ge p$. The noise-floor principle is thereby scoped: it bounds atomic uniform primitives, not derived or correlated samples.

Fourth, we analyse the **digit-convolution relaxation**. Linearizing the base-$b$ digit equations by $w_{ij} = p_iq_j$ makes factorizations exactly the rank-one solutions; the determinant, the constraint distinguishing them, is quadratic and hence discarded. We exhibit an explicit constant-norm kernel vector — the carry commutator $C = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, with $\Phi_b(C) = 0$ for all $b$ and $\|C\|^2 = 2$ — and deduce that every target has a non-rank-one companion solution at squared distance at most $8$, uniformly in $N$. Short-vector search cannot isolate the factorization.

We close with a tropical reformulation: in min-plus coordinates the divisor hyperbola degenerates to a line whose corner sits at $\sqrt N$, and every divisor pair straddles the corner. All four closures are stated and proved for all semiprimes, not as heuristics.

**Keywords:** semiprime, Legendre symbol, Jacobi symbol, character orthogonality, zero-divisor graph, complete bipartite graph, Pollard rho, pigeonhole, lattice relaxation, Gaussian heuristic, tropical geometry.

---

## 1. Introduction

Let $N = pq$ with $p \ne q$ prime. A **witness** for $N$ is any datum from which $p$ and $q$ can be recovered in time polynomial in $\log N$. Classical examples are numeric: the trace $p+q$; the larger factor $\max(p,q)$; the value $\varphi(N) = (p-1)(q-1)$; the order of the unit group; a nontrivial square root of $1$ modulo $N$. All of these are equivalent to the factorization, in both directions, by elementary algebra: from $s = p + q$ and $N = pq$ one solves $X^2 - sX + N = 0$; from $\varphi(N)$ one recovers $s = N + 1 - \varphi(N)$; and so on.

The interesting question is not whether other witnesses exist but whether there exist witnesses of a *genuinely different type* — objects that are not numbers of this classified kind, and whose evaluation might therefore evade the barriers that block the numeric ones. Four candidates, each with a plausible case for evading the classification, are the subject of this paper.

**(A) Symmetric character aggregates.** The known obstructions include a symmetry barrier: a quantity computable from $N$ alone is necessarily invariant under $p \leftrightarrow q$; conversely, many natural probes fail because they are *not* invariant and hence cannot be evaluated. This suggests searching for a probe that *is* invariant under all available symmetries and nevertheless separates semiprimes of equal size. The agreement set of Legendre symbols is the canonical candidate.

**(B) Structural (non-numeric) witnesses.** The classification of numeric witnesses says nothing, on its face, about *combinatorial* objects. A graph attached to $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ is not a number; if its isomorphism class determines $\{p,q\}$, then it is a witness outside the letter of the numeric classification.

**(C) Correlated samplers versus the noise floor.** A heuristic "noise-floor principle" asserts that factor-bearing events have density at most $\approx N^{-1/2}$. The sample set produced by the static rho iteration measurably violates the density form of this statement. Either the principle is false, or it must be scoped.

**(D) Geometry of numbers on the digits.** Digit-level multiplication is a convolution; linearizing it produces a lattice built from the digits of $N$ alone. If the factorization were the unique short vector of that lattice, lattice reduction would factor $N$.

We resolve all four. Each resolution is negative for factoring but positive as mathematics: each is an exact structural theorem about $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, valid for all semiprimes.

**Organization.** Section 2 fixes notation. Section 3 treats the agreement set. Section 4 determines the zero-divisor graph. Section 5 proves the atomic-uniform noise-floor bound and the rho correlation/aggregation dichotomy. Section 6 treats the digit lattice. Section 7 gives the tropical picture. Section 8 states the algorithmic consequences, Section 9 discusses scope and limitations, Section 10 lists future directions.

---

## 2. Notation and standing conventions

Throughout, $p$ and $q$ denote distinct primes and $N = pq$. We write:

- $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ for the unit group, of order $\varphi(N) = (p-1)(q-1)$;
- $\pi_p : \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_q : \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ for the reduction ring homomorphisms; by the Chinese Remainder Theorem $(\pi_p,\pi_q)$ is an isomorphism onto the product;
- $(a\mid p) \in \{0,\pm 1\}$ for the Legendre symbol, i.e. the unique quadratic character of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ extended by $0$; for $a$ a unit mod $N$, $(a\mid p)$ abbreviates the Legendre symbol of $\pi_p(a)$, and similarly for $q$;
- $J(a \mid N)$ for the Jacobi symbol, which for $N = pq$ satisfies $J(a\mid N) = (a\mid p)\,(a\mid q)$ by definition/multiplicativity in the lower argument, and which is computable in time $O(\log^2 N)$ from $a$ and $N$ alone, with no knowledge of $p,q$.

Since $\pi_p$ is a ring homomorphism and $a$ is a unit, $\pi_p(a)$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$; in particular $\pi_p(a) \ne 0$ and $(a\mid p) \in \{\pm1\}$. The same holds for $q$. We use this dichotomy repeatedly without comment.

---

## 3. Closure A: symmetric character aggregates collapse

### 3.1 The agreement set

**Definition 3.1 (Agreement set).** For $N = pq$,
$$A(N) \;=\; \bigl\{\, a \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times \;:\; (a\mid p) = (a\mid q) \,\bigr\}.$$

$A(N)$ is invariant under the swap $p \leftrightarrow q$ (the defining condition is symmetric) and under conjugation. It is therefore a legitimate candidate for a *both-symmetries-invariant* aggregate. The question is whether $|A(N)|$, or the set itself, separates factorizations.

### 3.2 The flipping unit

The engine of the collapse is a single element.

**Lemma 3.2 (Existence of a flipping unit).** Let $p$ be an odd prime and $q \ne p$ prime. Then there exists $u \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ with
$$(u \mid p) = -1, \qquad (u\mid q) = +1 .$$

*Proof.* Since $p$ is odd, the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is nontrivial, so there exists $y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $(y\mid p) = -1$; in particular $y \ne 0$. Since $p \ne q$ are primes they are coprime, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is an integer $k$ with $k \equiv y \pmod p$ and $k \equiv 1 \pmod q$. Then $p \nmid k$ (else $y = 0$) and $q \nmid k$ (else $1 \equiv 0 \bmod q$), so $\gcd(k, N) = 1$ and $k$ defines a unit $u$ of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. By construction $\pi_p(u) = y$, giving $(u\mid p) = -1$, and $\pi_q(u) = 1$, giving $(u \mid q) = +1$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.3 (Translation exchanges agreement and disagreement).** With $u$ as in Lemma 3.2, for every unit $a$:
$$a u \in A(N) \iff a \notin A(N).$$

*Proof.* Both Legendre symbols are multiplicative: $(au\mid p) = (a\mid p)(u\mid p) = -(a\mid p)$ and $(au\mid q) = (a\mid q)(u\mid q) = (a\mid q)$. Since $(a\mid p),(a\mid q) \in \{\pm1\}$, the equality $-(a\mid p) = (a\mid q)$ holds precisely when $(a\mid p) \neq (a\mid q)$. $\square$

### 3.3 The count

**Theorem 3.4 (Agreement collapse).** Let $p$ be an odd prime, $q \ne p$ prime, $N = pq$. Then
$$2\,|A(N)| \;=\; \varphi(N) \;=\; (p-1)(q-1),$$
that is, $|A(N)| = \varphi(N)/2$ exactly.

*Proof.* Right multiplication by the flipping unit $u$ is a bijection of $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ (its inverse is multiplication by $u^{-1}$). By Lemma 3.3 it carries $A(N)$ bijectively onto the complement $A(N)^c$ inside the unit group. Hence $|A(N)| = |A(N)^c|$. Since $|A(N)| + |A(N)^c| = |(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times| = \varphi(N)$, we get $2|A(N)| = \varphi(N)$. The explicit value follows from multiplicativity of $\varphi$ on coprime arguments and $\varphi(\text{prime } r) = r - 1$. $\square$

The count is a function of $\varphi(N)$ alone. Since $\varphi(N)$ is itself equivalent to the factorization ($p + q = N + 1 - \varphi(N)$), the count is not a *new* witness: it is the old one, and computing it requires already knowing the answer.

### 3.4 The collapse onto the Jacobi symbol

The set-level statement is stronger and more damning.

**Theorem 3.5 (Agreement is a Jacobi level set).** For every unit $a$ of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, with $\tilde a \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ its representative,
$$a \in A(N) \iff J(\tilde a \mid N) = 1 .$$

*Proof.* The Legendre symbol of $\pi_p(a)$ equals the Legendre symbol of the integer $\tilde a$ at $p$, since $\tilde a \equiv \pi_p(a) \bmod p$; likewise at $q$. By multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol in its lower argument, $J(\tilde a \mid pq) = (\tilde a\mid p)(\tilde a \mid q)$. Both factors lie in $\{\pm 1\}$, so their product is $+1$ exactly when they are equal, which is the definition of membership in $A(N)$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.6 (Barrier 2 in sharpest form).** The agreement aggregate is $N$-computable: membership in $A(N)$ is decidable in time $O(\log^2 N)$ from $N$ and $a$ alone. Hence it carries no information about $\{p,q\}$ beyond what $N$ already determines.

This is character orthogonality in action. The two Legendre characters $\chi_p = (\cdot \mid p)$ and $\chi_q = (\cdot\mid q)$, pulled back to $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, are distinct nontrivial quadratic characters. Any *aggregate* built from them that is invariant under the group $\{\mathrm{id},\ \chi_p \leftrightarrow \chi_q\}$ of available symmetries can only be a function of the product $\chi_p\chi_q$ — and the product is the Jacobi character mod $N$, which is public. Concretely, $\mathbf{1}[\chi_p(a) = \chi_q(a)] = \tfrac12(1 + \chi_p(a)\chi_q(a))$, an identity that displays the collapse in one line and, summed over $a$, reproves Theorem 3.4 since $\sum_a \chi_p(a)\chi_q(a) = 0$ by orthogonality of the nontrivial character $\chi_p\chi_q$.

## 4. Closure B: the zero-divisor graph is $K_{q-1,\,p-1}$, and it is circular

### 4.1 Vertices and wings

**Definition 4.1.** The **zero-divisor graph** $\Gamma(N)$ has vertex set
$$V(N) \;=\; \{\, x : 0 < x < N,\ \gcd(x, N) \ne 1 \,\},$$
and $x \sim y$ iff $x \ne y$ and $N \mid xy$.

**Definition 4.2.** For $d \mid N$, the **wing** of $d$ is $W_d = \{x : 0 < x < N,\ d \mid x\}$.

**Proposition 4.3 (Wing decomposition).** For distinct primes $p, q$ and $N = pq$:
$$V(N) = W_p \,\cup\, W_q, \qquad W_p \cap W_q = \emptyset .$$

*Proof.* If $x \in V(N)$ then $\gcd(x,N) > 1$, so some prime $r$ divides both $x$ and $N = pq$; as $r$ is prime, $r \in \{p, q\}$, placing $x$ in $W_p$ or $W_q$. Conversely if $p \mid x$ and $0<x<N$ then $p \mid \gcd(x,N)$, so $\gcd(x,N) \ne 1$; similarly for $q$. For disjointness: if $p \mid x$ and $q \mid x$ then, $p$ and $q$ being coprime, $N = pq \mid x$, forcing $x \ge N$ (as $x>0$), contradicting $x < N$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.4 (Wing sizes).** $|W_p| = q - 1$ and $|W_q| = p - 1$; hence
$$|V(N)| \;=\; p + q - 2 .$$

*Proof.* The map $k \mapsto pk$ is an injection from $\{1, \dots, q-1\}$ onto $W_p$: it lands in $W_p$ since $0 < pk < pq$, and every multiple of $p$ in $(0,N)$ has this form with $0 < k < q$. Injectivity is cancellation by $p > 0$. Symmetrically for $W_q$. The wings are disjoint, so the counts add, and $(q-1) + (p-1) = p+q-2$. $\square$

### 4.2 Exact adjacency: the graph is complete bipartite

**Theorem 4.5 (Bipartite structure).** Let $p \ne q$ be primes, $N = pq$. For $x, y \in V(N)$:
$$x \sim y \iff \bigl(x \in W_p \text{ and } y \in W_q\bigr) \ \text{or}\ \bigl(x \in W_q \text{ and } y \in W_p\bigr).$$
Equivalently, $\Gamma(N) \cong K_{q-1,\,p-1}$: it is the complete bipartite graph on parts of sizes $q-1$ and $p-1$.

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) If $x = pa$ and $y = qb$ then $xy = pq\,ab$, so $N \mid xy$; and $x \ne y$ because the wings are disjoint.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $x, y$ lie in the *same* wing, say both in $W_p$, and $N \mid xy$. Then $q \mid xy$, and $q$ prime gives $q \mid x$ or $q \mid y$. Either way that element lies in $W_p \cap W_q = \emptyset$, a contradiction. The argument for $W_q$ is symmetric (swap the roles of $p$ and $q$). Since by Proposition 4.3 every vertex lies in one of the two wings, the only remaining possibility for an edge is a cross-wing pair. $\square$

**Corollary 4.6 (Degrees).** Every $x \in W_p$ has $\deg(x) = |W_q| = p-1$, and every $x \in W_q$ has $\deg(x) = |W_p| = q-1$. Consequently, for every vertex $x$,
$$\deg(x) + 1 \in \{p, q\} \quad\text{and}\quad (\deg(x)+1) \mid N .$$

Thus the degree sequence of $\Gamma(N)$ — indeed the degree of a *single* vertex — recovers the factorization. This is precisely the sense in which a structural witness exists: $\Gamma(N)$ is a combinatorial object, not a number in the classified list, and its isomorphism class determines $\{p, q\}$.

### 4.3 The structural witness is the trace witness

**Theorem 4.7 (Collapse onto the trace).** Set $s = |V(N)| + 2$. Then $s = p + q$, and both primes are roots of
$$X^2 - sX + N = 0 .$$

*Proof.* Proposition 4.4 gives $|V(N)| = p+q-2$, so $s = p+q$. Then $p^2 - (p+q)p + pq = 0$ and $q^2 - (p+q)q + pq = 0$ identically. $\square$

So whatever novelty the graph possesses as an *object*, the information it delivers is exactly the classical trace $p+q$. The structural witness does not escape the numeric classification; it re-encodes it.

### 4.4 The circularity

**Theorem 4.8 (Circularity of the structural witness).** For every $x \in V(N)$,
$$\gcd(x, N) \in \{p, q\} .$$
In particular, exhibiting a single vertex of $\Gamma(N)$ already exhibits a nontrivial factor of $N$, at the cost of one gcd.

*Proof.* Let $x \in W_p$ (the case $x \in W_q$ is symmetric). Then $p \mid x$ and $p \mid N$, so $p \mid g := \gcd(x,N)$; write $g = pk$. From $g \mid N = pq$ and cancellation, $k \mid q$, so $k = 1$ or $k = q$ by primality. If $k = q$ then $q \mid g \mid x$, placing $x \in W_p \cap W_q = \emptyset$ — impossible. Hence $k=1$ and $g = p$. $\square$

**Corollary 4.9 (Cost of construction).** The vertex set $V(N)$ has density $(p+q-2)/N$ inside $[1,N)$. Locating a vertex by search over residues is exactly the trial-division / uniform-sampling problem of Section 5, and by Theorem 5.2 succeeds with probability at most $2/\min(p,q)$ per query. Hence *building* $\Gamma(N)$ costs $\Omega(\min(p,q))$ queries in the worst case, whereas *reading* it (via Corollary 4.6) is free.

This is the precise verdict: the structural witness is real, lies outside the letter of the numeric classification, and is nonetheless sealed — not by the classification but by the conjunction of aggregation cost (Corollary 4.9) and circularity (Theorem 4.8).

## 5. Closure C: scoping the noise-floor principle

### 5.1 The atomic uniform primitive

**Definition 5.1.** The **hit density** of $N = pq$ is
$$\delta(N) \;=\; \frac{|V(N)|}{N} \;=\; \frac{p+q-2}{pq},$$
the probability that a single uniform draw $a \leftarrow [1, N)$ satisfies $\gcd(a,N) > 1$.

**Theorem 5.2 (Atomic uniform noise-floor bound).** If $p \le q$ then
$$\delta(N) \;\le\; \frac{2}{p} \;=\; \frac{2}{\min(p,q)} .$$

*Proof.* $\delta(N) = (p+q-2)/(pq)$. Since $p \le q$ we have $p + q - 2 < 2q$, hence $\delta(N) < 2q/(pq) = 2/p$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.3 (The floor and its extremal case).** For all naturals $p,q$: $(p+q)^2 \ge 4pq$, with equality iff $p = q$. Consequently, writing $\delta = \delta(N)$,
$$\bigl(\delta N + 2\bigr)^2 \;\ge\; 4N,$$
so $\delta \ge (2\sqrt N - 2)/N$: the hit density is bounded below by roughly $2/\sqrt N$, with the minimum approached exactly at balanced semiprimes.

*Proof.* $(p+q)^2 - 4pq = (p-q)^2 \ge 0$, vanishing iff $p=q$. For the second statement, $\delta N = p+q-2$, so $(\delta N + 2)^2 = (p+q)^2 \ge 4pq = 4N$. $\square$

Theorems 5.2 and 5.3 pin the atomic uniform primitive between $2/\sqrt N$ (balanced case, the hard case, and the cryptographic case) and $2/\min(p,q)$ (unbalanced case, where trial division is cheap anyway). This is the **noise-floor principle**, and in this form it is a theorem.

### 5.2 The static rho sampler: correlation beats density

Now consider the *derived* sample set generated by iterating a polynomial map. Let
$$\rho(x) = x^2 + 1 ,$$
taken over $\mathbb{Z}$ so that differences of iterates make sense, and let $x_t = \rho^{[t]}(x_0)$.

**Lemma 5.4 (Reduction-compatibility).** For any modulus $m$ and any $a \equiv b \pmod m$, we have $\rho(a) \equiv \rho(b) \pmod m$, and hence by induction $\rho^{[t]}(a) \equiv \rho^{[t]}(b) \pmod m$ for all $t \ge 0$.

*Proof.* Congruence is preserved by multiplication and addition: $a\equiv b$ gives $a^2 \equiv b^2$ and then $a^2+1 \equiv b^2 + 1$. Induction on $t$, applying the one-step statement to the congruent pair $\rho^{[t]}(a) \equiv \rho^{[t]}(b)$. $\square$

The lemma is the source of the correlation: the walk modulo $N$ *covers* the walk modulo $p$. The reduced walk lives in a state space of size $p$, not $N$, and this alone forces structure.

**Theorem 5.5 (Unconditional collision).** Let $p \ge 1$ and let $x_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ be arbitrary. There exist $i < j \le p$ with
$$p \mid x_j - x_i .$$
No probabilistic hypothesis is used.

*Proof.* Consider the map $t \mapsto x_t \bmod p$ on $\{0,1,\dots,p\}$, a set of $p+1$ indices, taking values in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, a set of $p$ values. By pigeonhole it is not injective: there are indices $i \ne j$ in $\{0,\dots,p\}$ with $x_i \equiv x_j \pmod p$. Order them so that $i<j$; then $j \le p$ and $p \mid x_j - x_i$. $\square$

**Lemma 5.6 (Extraction).** Let $p,q$ be primes and $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $p \mid d$ and $q \nmid d$. Then
$$\gcd(d, pq) = p .$$

*Proof.* Let $g = \gcd(d, pq)$. From $p \mid d$ and $p \mid pq$ we get $p \mid g$; write $g = pk$. From $g \mid pq$ and cancellation, $k \mid q$, so $k \in \{1,q\}$. If $k = q$ then $q \mid g \mid d$, contradicting $q \nmid d$. Hence $g = p$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.7 (Correctness core of the rho method).** For any $x_0$ and any distinct primes $p,q$, there exist $i<j\le p$ with $p \mid x_j - x_i$, and for any such pair, if additionally $q \nmid x_j - x_i$, then
$$\gcd(x_j - x_i,\ N) = p .$$

*Proof.* Combine Theorem 5.5 and Lemma 5.6. $\square$

Thus the factor-bearing density of the rho sample *set* is not $N^{-1/2}$: among $T = p+1$ samples a factor-bearing pair is guaranteed, i.e. the pair-density is at least $1/\binom{p+1}{2}$ and the *set*-level success probability is $1$. The density form of the noise-floor principle is therefore false for correlated samples — as experiment measured directly.

### 5.3 The aggregation price

**Theorem 5.8 (Aggregation cost).** For every $p \ge 0$,
$$\binom{p+1}{2} \;=\; \frac{p(p+1)}{2} \;\ge\; p .$$

*Proof.* For $p = 0$ both sides are $0$. For $p \ge 1$, $p(p+1)/2 \ge p \iff p+1 \ge 2$, true. $\square$

**Corollary 5.9 (Scoping of the noise-floor principle).** Extracting a factor from the guaranteed collision of Theorem 5.7 by unstructured pairwise gcds requires $\binom{T}{2}$ operations with $T = p+1$, hence at least $p$ operations — no fewer than trial division by all primes up to $p$. The density gain of the correlated sample set is therefore not a complexity gain.

The correct statement of the principle is consequently:

> **Noise-floor principle (scoped).** The bound $\Pr[\text{success}] \le 2/\min(p,q)$ applies to an *atomic uniform primitive*: a single query drawn from the uniform distribution on $[1,N)$ (or a distribution close to it). It is *not* a density theorem about derived or correlated sample sets. Correlated sets may have far higher factor-bearing density; what they do not evade is the cost of the aggregation needed to convert density into a factor.

The genuine $\tilde O(\sqrt p)$ running time of Pollard's rho comes from replacing exhaustive pairwise comparison by cycle detection together with a birthday heuristic on the reduced functional graph — a *known method*, and the recognized exception to the principle, not a new escape from it.

## 6. Closure D: the digit relaxation is degenerate

### 6.1 The relaxation

Fix a base $b \ge 2$ and consider two-digit factors $p = u_0 + u_1 b$, $q = v_0 + v_1 b$ (the smallest nontrivial case; the phenomenon below is dimension-independent, since the kernel vector we construct is supported on two coordinates).

Multiplication is a digit convolution. Introducing the relaxation variables $w_{ij} = u_iv_j$ makes the digit equations linear, with the number recovered by the **digit functional**
$$\Phi_b(w) \;=\; \sum_{i,j\in\{0,1\}} w_{ij}\, b^{\,i+j} .$$
Write $\langle u\rangle_b = u_0 + u_1b$ and let $u \otimes v$ denote the rank-one matrix $(u_iv_j)_{i,j}$. Let $\|w\|^2 = \sum_{i,j} w_{ij}^2$ be the squared Frobenius norm.

**Proposition 6.1 (Faithfulness).** $\Phi_b(u\otimes v) = \langle u\rangle_b\,\langle v\rangle_b$.

*Proof.* $\sum_{i,j} u_iv_j b^{i+j} = \bigl(\sum_i u_ib^i\bigr)\bigl(\sum_j v_jb^j\bigr)$. $\square$

So the solutions of $\Phi_b(w) = N$ that are *rank one with the right digit ranges* are exactly the factorizations of $N$. The relaxation drops the rank condition.

**Proposition 6.2 (The discarded constraint).** $\det(u\otimes v) = (u_0v_0)(u_1v_1) - (u_0v_1)(u_1v_0) = 0$. Rank-one matrices are exactly those killed by the determinant, a *quadratic* function; the linear relaxation cannot express it.

### 6.2 The carry commutator

**Definition 6.3.** The **carry commutator** is $C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$.

**Theorem 6.4 (Kernel vector of constant norm).** For every base $b$,
$$\Phi_b(C) = b^{0+1} - b^{1+0} = 0, \qquad \|C\|^2 = 2 .$$

The reason is structural: the coefficient $b^{i+j}$ depends only on $i+j$, so the functional cannot distinguish the transposed positions $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$. The information lost in that identification is exactly the carry information of the original digit multiplication.

**Theorem 6.5 (Non-isolation of the factorization target).** For every base $b$ and all digit vectors $u,v$, there exists an integer matrix $w$ with
$$\Phi_b(w) = \Phi_b(u\otimes v), \qquad \det w \ne 0, \qquad \|w - u\otimes v\|^2 \le 8 .$$
In particular $w$ solves the relaxed digit system for the same $N$ but is *not* a factorization, and its distance from the target is bounded by an absolute constant independent of $N$.

*Proof.* Take $w = u\otimes v + cC$ for $c \in \{1,2\}$. Then $\Phi_b(w) = \Phi_b(u\otimes v) + c\,\Phi_b(C) = \Phi_b(u\otimes v)$ by Theorem 6.4, and $\|w - u\otimes v\|^2 = c^2\|C\|^2 = 2c^2 \le 8$. For the determinant, a direct $2\times2$ computation with $D = u_0v_1 - u_1v_0$ gives
$$\det(u\otimes v + cC) = c\,D + c^2 .$$
If $D + 1 \ne 0$, take $c = 1$: the determinant is $D + 1 \ne 0$. If $D + 1 = 0$, i.e. $D = -1$, take $c = 2$: the determinant is $2(-1) + 4 = 2 \ne 0$. $\square$

**Proposition 6.6 (Target norm grows).** $\|u\otimes v\|^2 = (u_0^2+u_1^2)(v_0^2+v_1^2)$; in particular if all four digits are nonzero then $\|u \otimes v\|^2 \ge 4$, and the norm grows multiplicatively with the digit norms of $p$ and $q$.

**Corollary 6.7 (Failure of short-vector search).** The relaxed solution set contains, within an $O(1)$-radius ball around every factorization target, spurious solutions of the same digit value with nonzero determinant. Since the target's own norm grows with the size of $N$ while the perturbation stays of constant size, the factorization is never an isolated shortest vector; a reduction algorithm returning a shortest or nearly-shortest vector has no mechanism to prefer the rank-one point. This is the exact structural content of the observation that the target sits *at* the Gaussian heuristic $\sqrt{\dim}$ rather than well below it.

Re-imposing rank one is not a repair: rank one plus carry integrality is the $\Theta(N)$-state de-carrying dynamic program, which is not a relaxation at all but the original problem restated.

## 7. The tropical picture: the corner at $\sqrt N$

All four closures share a geometric shadow. The divisor locus of $N$ is the hyperbola $xy = N$. Passing to logarithms turns it into the line
$$X + Y = \log N .$$
In the min-plus (tropical) semiring, where $a \oplus b = \min(a,b)$ and $a \odot b = a+b$, the tropical polynomial $X \odot Y$ is ordinary addition, and the tropical line $X\odot Y = \log N$ has its corner — the point of symmetry, where the two coordinates are equal — at $X = Y = \tfrac12 \log N$, i.e. at $\sqrt N$.

**Proposition 7.1 (Corner straddle).** If $p \le q$ and $N = pq$ then $p^2 \le N \le q^2$. In logarithmic coordinates, $\log p \le \tfrac12\log N \le \log q$: every divisor pair straddles the corner.

*Proof.* Multiply $p \le q$ by $p > 0$ and by $q>0$ respectively. $\square$

**Proposition 7.2 (Tropical submultiplicativity of the integer logarithm).** For primes $p,q$, in min-plus coordinates with $\lfloor \log_2 \cdot \rfloor$,
$$\lfloor \log_2 p\rfloor \odot \lfloor \log_2 q \rfloor \;\le\; \lfloor \log_2 (pq)\rfloor,$$
i.e. $\lfloor\log_2 p\rfloor + \lfloor \log_2 q\rfloor \le \lfloor \log_2 N\rfloor$; and the tropical *sum* (the minimum) of the two coordinates is at most the corner coordinate $\tfrac12\log_2 N$.

*Proof.* $2^{\lfloor\log_2 p\rfloor}\cdot 2^{\lfloor\log_2 q\rfloor} \le pq$, so the exponent sum is at most $\lfloor\log_2(pq)\rfloor$ by the defining property of the integer logarithm. The second statement is the straddle of Proposition 7.1 in logarithmic form. $\square$

The corner is the geometric form of the noise floor: the balanced case $p \approx q \approx \sqrt N$ is where the divisor locus is furthest from the coordinate axes and where the hit density of Theorem 5.3 attains its minimum $\approx 2/\sqrt N$. Each of the four probes above is, in this language, an attempt to reach the corner along a path that does not cross the $\sqrt N$ scale. None succeeds.

## 8. Algorithms and their costs

We record the algorithmic content of the results, with complexity in bit operations, $n = \log_2 N$.

**Algorithm 1 (Agreement test).** Given $N$ and $a$: return $[\,J(a\mid N) = 1\,]$, computed by the quadratic-reciprocity Euclidean algorithm. Cost $O(n^2)$. By Theorem 3.5 this decides membership in $A(N)$ *without* knowing $p,q$; by Theorem 3.4 the aggregate count is $\varphi(N)/2$, so no query strategy against $A(N)$ can separate two semiprimes of equal $\varphi$-value.

**Algorithm 2 (Zero-divisor graph reader).** Given a vertex $x$: output $\gcd(x,N)$, which by Theorem 4.8 is $p$ or $q$; or output $\deg(x)+1$, which by Corollary 4.6 is $p$ or $q$. Cost $O(n^2)$ *given* the vertex. Producing the vertex costs $\Omega(\min(p,q))$ expected queries by Theorem 5.2 — the entire cost of the pipeline is in the input.

**Algorithm 3 (Unconditional rho collision).** Iterate $x \mapsto x^2 + 1 \bmod N$ for $T$ steps, storing all iterates; for each pair $(i,j)$ compute $g=\gcd(x_j - x_i, N)$ and return $g$ if $1 < g < N$. By Theorem 5.7 the algorithm succeeds with $T = p + 1$; the pairwise loop costs $\binom{T}{2} = \Theta(p^2)$ gcds. Floyd cycle detection reduces the loop to $O(T)$ gcds but reintroduces a heuristic (birthday) bound $T \approx \sqrt p$; that is the known-method exception.

**Algorithm 4 (Digit-lattice perturbation certificate).** Given a base $b$ and a candidate rank-one target $u\otimes v$, output $w = u\otimes v + cC$ with $c \in \{1,2\}$ chosen so that $cD + c^2 \ne 0$, where $D = u_0v_1 - u_1v_0$. By Theorem 6.5 this is a same-value, non-rank-one lattice point at squared distance $\le 8$. Cost $O(1)$ arithmetic operations. The certificate demonstrates non-isolation *for the specific target*, hence rules out short-vector search as an isolation mechanism.

## 9. Discussion

### 9.1 Four distinct failure modes

It is worth emphasizing that the four closures fail for four genuinely different reasons.

- **Symmetry saturation (Section 3).** An aggregate invariant under all symmetries available to a $p,q$-agnostic observer becomes computable by that observer. This is a statement about characters and orthogonality; nothing about computation enters except the observation that $J(\cdot\mid N)$ is fast.
- **Access, not information (Section 4).** The zero-divisor graph *does* contain the factorization, redundantly and in a form outside the numeric classification. The obstruction is that its vertex set coincides with the divisor structure, so it cannot be constructed without solving the problem. This is the cleanest available example of a witness that is real, non-numeric, and useless.
- **Scope of a probabilistic bound (Section 5).** A bound proved for one sampling model was applied to another. The repair is a scoping statement, and the resulting picture is *sharper* than the original: the atomic bound is now a theorem with explicit constant $2/\min(p,q)$, and the correlated regime is characterized by the aggregation cost.
- **Relaxation degeneracy (Section 6).** Convexifying/linearizing a rank constraint creates a kernel; if the kernel contains a constant-norm lattice vector, the relaxed problem cannot isolate the true point. This is a general lesson about lattice attacks on multiplicative structure, not specific to base $b$ or to two digits.

### 9.2 What the closures do *not* show

None of these results is a lower bound on the complexity of integer factorization, and none should be read as evidence that no polynomial algorithm exists. They are exact statements about four specific probes. In particular:

- Theorem 3.4 does not preclude a *non*-symmetric aggregate being useful; it shows that symmetry buys nothing.
- Theorem 4.5 does not preclude *other* structural witnesses; it shows that this one is circular. A structural witness whose construction does not require a nontrivial divisor is not ruled out by anything here.
- Theorem 5.2 bounds a single query; it says nothing about adaptive multi-query strategies except through the aggregation accounting.
- Theorem 6.5 rules out short-vector isolation for the specific two-digit relaxation with the digit functional $\Phi_b$; a relaxation with a genuinely different linear functional, or with a lattice in which the transpose degeneracy is broken, is not addressed.

### 9.3 The unifying accounting

A common ledger runs through all four. Every probe has an *evaluation cost* and an *information content*. The classified numeric witnesses have low evaluation cost only when the answer is known. What the four closures show is that each of the new candidates satisfies one of:

$$\text{(i) information content } = 0, \qquad \text{(ii) evaluation cost } \ge \min(p,q), \qquad \text{(iii) target not isolated.}$$

The agreement set falls in (i); the zero-divisor graph in (ii); the rho sample set in (ii) via aggregation; the digit lattice in (iii). There is no candidate here in the desired regime of positive information at polylogarithmic cost.

## 10. Future directions

The exact structural theorems proved above suggest sharper, falsifiable successors.

**Conjecture A (Structural-witness dichotomy).** For every pair of distinct primes $p \ne q$, any graph invariant of the zero-divisor graph of $\mathbb{Z}/pq\mathbb{Z}$ that is computable in time $\mathrm{polylog}\,N$ from $N$ alone is a function of $N$ alone; equivalently, every invariant that separates two semiprimes of equal size requires $\Omega(\min(p,q))$ vertex queries. The motivation is Theorem 4.8: a *single* vertex already yields a factor, so an invariant is either blind (a function of $N$) or its evaluation embeds trial division — there is no middle regime. With the graph now characterized exactly as $K_{q-1,p-1}$ with a proven degree sequence, query-complexity statements about it can be attacked directly.

**Conjecture B (Atomic-uniform noise floor as a theorem, not a principle).** Let $D$ be any distribution on $[1,N)$ whose density is computable from $N$ in $\mathrm{polylog}\,N$ time and which is $\varepsilon$-close to uniform in total variation. Then a single sample from $D$ reveals a nontrivial factor with probability at most $2/\min(p,q) + \varepsilon$. Theorem 5.2 is the uniform case with exact constant $2/p$, and the perturbation term is forced by the total-variation bound; the content is that polylog-computability prevents any density from concentrating on the $p+q-2$ zero divisors.

**Conjecture C (Aggregation lower bound for correlated samplers).** Any algorithm that factors $N = pq$ using only pairwise gcds of iterates of a degree-$d$ polynomial map mod $N$ must perform $\Omega(\sqrt p)$ gcd operations, and the $p+1$ pigeonhole bound of Theorem 5.5 is tight up to the birthday square root.     print("\nThe density is smallest exactly when p = q (balanced semiprimes):")

    """Iterates of the static rho map x -> x^2 + 1 reduced mod n."""
    out = [x0 % n]
    for _ in range(steps):

    return out

    xs = rho_iterates(x0, n, p + 1)

    ys = rho_iterates(x0, p, p + 1)

    # Pigeonhole: a collision mod p among the first p+1 iterates.

    for i, j in combinations(range(p + 1), 2):

    extracted = None
    for i, j in combinations(range(p + 1), 2):
        g = gcd(abs(xs[j] - xs[i]), n)
        if 1 < g < n:

    print("3b. CORRELATED RHO SAMPLER:  guaranteed collision, priced by aggregation")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"   N = {p} * {q} = {n},  walk x -> x^2 + 1,  x0 = {x0}")

    print(f"   the same walk mod p : {ys[:8]} ...   (reduction-compatibility)")
    i, j = collision

    if extracted:

        print(f"   extraction: gcd(x_{j} - x_{i}, N) = {g}  (a nontrivial factor)")

    print("\n   Density is NOT the obstruction for correlated samples; cost is.\n")

Matrix2 = Tuple[Tuple[int, int], Tuple[int, int]]

CARRY_COMMUTATOR: Matrix2 = ((0, 1), (-1, 0))


def digit_val(b: int, w: Matrix2) -> int:
    """The digit functional Phi_b(w) = sum_{i,j} w_ij b^{i+j}."""
    return sum(w[i][j] * b ** (i + j) for i in range(2) for j in range(2))

    """The rank-one target u (x) v with entries u_i v_j."""
    return ((u[0] * v[0], u[0] * v[1]), (u[1] * v[0], u[1] * v[1]))


def det2(w: Matrix2) -> int:
    return w[0][0] * w[1][1] - w[0][1] * w[1][0]


def sq_norm(w: Matrix2) -> int:
    return sum(w[i][j] ** 2 for i in range(2) for j in range(2))


def add_scaled(w: Matrix2, c: int, m: Matrix2) -> Matrix2:
    return tuple(tuple(w[i][j] + c * m[i][j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2))  # type: ignore[return-value]


def spurious_companion(u: Tuple[int, int], v: Tuple[int, int]) -> Tuple[Matrix2, int]:

    d = u[0] * v[1] - u[1] * v[0]

    return (x % b, x // b)

    print(f"4. DIGIT LATTICE (base {b}): the target is never isolated")
    print("=" * 74)
    assert digit_val(b, CARRY_COMMUTATOR) == 0
    assert sq_norm(CARRY_COMMUTATOR) == 2
    print(f"   carry commutator C = {CARRY_COMMUTATOR}: "
          f"Phi_b(C) = {digit_val(b, CARRY_COMMUTATOR)}, ||C||^2 = {sq_norm(CARRY_COMMUTATOR)}")
    print(f"{'p':>5} {'q':>5} {'N':>7} {'Phi(target)':>12} {'Phi(spurious)':>14}"
          f" {'det':>6} {'dist^2':>7} {'||target||^2':>13}")
    for p, q in factor_pairs:

        assert det2(target) == 0

        assert digit_val(b, w) == digit_val(b, target)
        assert det2(w) != 0
        assert dist <= 8
        print(f"{p:>5} {q:>5} {p*q:>7} {digit_val(b, target):>12} {digit_val(b, w):>14}"

    print("   norm grows with the digits: short-vector search cannot separate them.\n")

    print("=" * 74)

              f" {(n.bit_length()-1)/2:>11.1f} {hi.bit_length()-1:>9}")
    print("\n   In min-plus coordinates the hyperbola xy = N is a line whose corner")
    print("   sits at sqrt(N); the noise floor 2/sqrt(N) is that corner.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# main
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    small_pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(3, 5), (3, 7), (5, 7), (5, 11), (7, 11), (11, 13)]
    big_pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [

    demo_tropical_corner(small_pairs + big_pairs)

    print("=" * 74)
    print("All assertions passed: every closure verified on explicit numbers.")
    print("=" * 74)

    main()

        assert len(a_set) == half_phi, "agreement count must be phi(N)/2"
        assert a_set == j_set, "agreement set must be the Jacobi level set"
        print(f"{p:>5} {q:>5} {p*q:>8} {len(a_set):>8} {half_phi:>9} {'yes':>15}")
    print("\nThe count depends only on phi(N), and membership is decidable from N")
    print("alone by the Jacobi symbol: the aggregate carries no extra information.\n")


def demo_flipping_unit(p: int, q: int) -> None:
    """Exhibit the CRT witness u with (u|p) = -1, (u|q) = +1 driving the pairing."""
    n = p * q
    u = next(a for a in units_mod(n)
             if legendre_symbol(a, p) == -1 and legendre_symbol(a, q) == 1)
    a_set = set(agreement_set(p, q))
    images = {(a * u) % n for a in a_set}
    complement = set(units_mod(n)) - a_set
    assert images == complement, "multiplication by u must swap A(N) and its complement"
    print(f"   flipping unit for N = {p}*{q} = {n}:  u = {u}"
          f"   (u mod p = {u % p}, u mod q = {u % q})")
    print(f"   u maps A(N) bijectively onto its complement: "
          f"{len(a_set)} <-> {len(complement)}\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. THE ZERO-DIVISOR GRAPH
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def zd_vertices(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Nonzero zero-divisors of Z/nZ: 0 < x < n with gcd(x, n) > 1."""
    return [x for x in range(1, n) if gcd(x, n) != 1]


def zd_adjacency(n: int, vertices: Sequence[int]) -> Dict[int, List[int]]:
    """Adjacency lists: x ~ y iff x != y and n | x*y."""
    return {x: [y for y in vertices if y != x and (x * y) % n == 0] for x in vertices}


def demo_zero_divisor_graph(p: int, q: int) -> None:
    n = p * q
    verts = zd_vertices(n)
    wing_p = [x for x in verts if x % p == 0]
    wing_q = [x for x in verts if x % q == 0]
    adj = zd_adjacency(n, verts)

    assert len(verts) == p + q - 2
    assert len(wing_p) == q - 1 and len(wing_q) == p - 1
    assert not (set(wing_p) & set(wing_q))

    # complete bipartite: edge iff opposite wings
    for x, y in combinations(verts, 2):
        cross = (x % p == 0) != (y % p == 0)
        assert (y in adj[x]) == cross

    # degrees and circularity
    for x in verts:
        d = len(adj[x])
        assert d + 1 in (p, q) and n % (d + 1) == 0
        assert gcd(x, n) in (p, q)

    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. ZERO-DIVISOR GRAPH of Z/NZ  is  K_{q-1, p-1}")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"   N = {p} * {q} = {n}")
    print(f"   |V| = {len(verts)} = p + q - 2 = {p + q - 2}   (trace witness: p+q = {p+q})")
    print(f"   p-wing (multiples of {p}): {wing_p}   size {len(wing_p)} = q - 1")
    print(f"   q-wing (multiples of {q}): {wing_q}   size {len(wing_q)} = p - 1")
    example = verts[0]
    print(f"   degree of vertex {example}: {len(adj[example])}"
          f"  ->  {len(adj[example]) + 1} divides N")
    print(f"   circularity: gcd({example}, N) = {gcd(example, n)}"
          f"  -- one vertex already gives a factor")
    s = len(verts) + 2
    disc = isqrt(s * s - 4 * n)
    print(f"   roots of X^2 - {s}X + {n}:  {(s - disc)//2} and {(s + disc)//2}\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. NOISE FLOOR AND THE CORRELATED RHO SAMPLER
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def hit_density(p: int, q: int) -> float:
    """Probability that a single uniform draw from [1,N) exposes a factor."""
    return (p + q - 2) / (p * q)


def demo_noise_floor(pairs: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3a. ATOMIC UNIFORM NOISE FLOOR:  delta(N) = (p+q-2)/N <= 2/min(p,q)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'p':>7} {'q':>7} {'N':>11} {'delta(N)':>12} {'2/min(p,q)':>12} {'2/sqrt(N)':>12}")
    for p, q in pairs:
        d = hit_density(p, q)
        upper = 2 / min(p, q)
        floor = 2 / (p * q) ** 0.5
        assert d <= upper + 1e-15
        assert (p + q) ** 2 >= 4 * p * q
        assert d >= floor - 2 / (p * q)
        print(f"{p:>7} {q:>7} {p*q:>11} {d:>12.3e} {upper:>12.3e} {floor:>12.3e}")
    print("\nThe density is smallest exactly when p = q (balanced semiprimes):")
    print("(p+q)^2 - 4pq = (p-q)^2 >= 0, with equality iff p = q.\n")


def rho_iterates(x0: int, n: int, steps: int) -> List[int]:
    """Iterates of the static rho map x -> x^2 + 1 reduced mod n."""
    out = [x0 % n]
    for _ in range(steps):
        out.append((out[-1] * out[-1] + 1) % n)
    return out


def demo_rho_collision(p: int, q: int, x0: int = 2) -> None:
    n = p * q
    xs = rho_iterates(x0, n, p + 1)

    # Reduction-compatibility: the mod-N walk covers the mod-p walk.
    ys = rho_iterates(x0, p, p + 1)
    assert [x % p for x in xs] == ys

    # Pigeonhole: a collision mod p among the first p+1 iterates.
    collision = None
    for i, j in combinations(range(p + 1), 2):
        if (xs[j] - xs[i]) % p == 0:
            collision = (i, j)
            break
    assert collision is not None, "pigeonhole guarantees a collision mod p"

    # Extraction: a one-sided collision returns the factor exactly.
    extracted = None
    for i, j in combinations(range(p + 1), 2):
        g = gcd(abs(xs[j] - xs[i]), n)
        if 1 < g < n:
            extracted = (i, j, g)
            break

    print("=" * 74)
    print("3b. CORRELATED RHO SAMPLER:  guaranteed collision, priced by aggregation")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"   N = {p} * {q} = {n},  walk x -> x^2 + 1,  x0 = {x0}")
    print(f"   first iterates mod N: {xs[:8]} ...")
    print(f"   the same walk mod p : {ys[:8]} ...   (reduction-compatibility)")
    i, j = collision
    print(f"   pigeonhole collision at (i, j) = ({i}, {j}) <= p = {p}: "
          f"p divides x_j - x_i")
    if extracted:
        i, j, g = extracted
        print(f"   extraction: gcd(x_{j} - x_{i}, N) = {g}  (a nontrivial factor)")
    pairs_needed = (p + 1) * p // 2
    print(f"   aggregation cost: C(p+1, 2) = {pairs_needed} >= p = {p} "
          f"gcds -- at least trial division")
    print("\n   Density is NOT the obstruction for correlated samples; cost is.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. DIGIT-LATTICE NON-ISOLATION
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

Matrix2 = Tuple[Tuple[int, int], Tuple[int, int]]

CARRY_COMMUTATOR: Matrix2 = ((0, 1), (-1, 0))


def digit_val(b: int, w: Matrix2) -> int:
    """The digit functional Phi_b(w) = sum_{i,j} w_ij b^{i+j}."""
    return sum(w[i][j] * b ** (i + j) for i in range(2) for j in range(2))


def rank_one(u: Tuple[int, int], v: Tuple[int, int]) -> Matrix2:
    """The rank-one target u (x) v with entries u_i v_j."""
    return ((u[0] * v[0], u[0] * v[1]), (u[1] * v[0], u[1] * v[1]))


def det2(w: Matrix2) -> int:
    return w[0][0] * w[1][1] - w[0][1] * w[1][0]


def sq_norm(w: Matrix2) -> int:
    return sum(w[i][j] ** 2 for i in range(2) for j in range(2))


def add_scaled(w: Matrix2, c: int, m: Matrix2) -> Matrix2:
    return tuple(tuple(w[i][j] + c * m[i][j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2))  # type: ignore[return-value]


def spurious_companion(u: Tuple[int, int], v: Tuple[int, int]) -> Tuple[Matrix2, int]:
    """A same-value, nonzero-determinant lattice point near the target u (x) v."""
    d = u[0] * v[1] - u[1] * v[0]
    c = 1 if d + 1 != 0 else 2
    return add_scaled(rank_one(u, v), c, CARRY_COMMUTATOR), c


def digits_base(x: int, b: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    return (x % b, x // b)


def demo_digit_lattice(b: int, factor_pairs: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"4. DIGIT LATTICE (base {b}): the target is never isolated")
    print("=" * 74)
    assert digit_val(b, CARRY_COMMUTATOR) == 0
    assert sq_norm(CARRY_COMMUTATOR) == 2
    print(f"   carry commutator C = {CARRY_COMMUTATOR}: "
          f"Phi_b(C) = {digit_val(b, CARRY_COMMUTATOR)}, ||C||^2 = {sq_norm(CARRY_COMMUTATOR)}")
    print(f"{'p':>5} {'q':>5} {'N':>7} {'Phi(target)':>12} {'Phi(spurious)':>14}"
          f" {'det':>6} {'dist^2':>7} {'||target||^2':>13}")
    for p, q in factor_pairs:
        u, v = digits_base(p, b), digits_base(q, b)
        target = rank_one(u, v)
        assert digit_val(b, target) == p * q
        assert det2(target) == 0
        w, c = spurious_companion(u, v)
        dist = sq_norm(add_scaled(w, -1, target))
        assert digit_val(b, w) == digit_val(b, target)
        assert det2(w) != 0
        assert dist <= 8
        print(f"{p:>5} {q:>5} {p*q:>7} {digit_val(b, target):>12} {digit_val(b, w):>14}"
              f" {det2(w):>6} {dist:>7} {sq_norm(target):>13}")
    print("\n   The impostor stays at squared distance <= 8 while the target's own")
    print("   norm grows with the digits: short-vector search cannot separate them.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. THE TROPICAL CORNER
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_tropical_corner(pairs: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. TROPICAL CORNER: every divisor pair straddles sqrt(N)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'p':>7} {'q':>7} {'N':>11} {'log2 p':>9} {'log2 N / 2':>11} {'log2 q':>9}")
    for p, q in pairs:
        lo, hi = min(p, q), max(p, q)
        n = p * q
        assert lo * lo <= n <= hi * hi
        assert (lo.bit_length() - 1) + (hi.bit_length() - 1) <= n.bit_length() - 1
        print(f"{lo:>7} {hi:>7} {n:>11} {lo.bit_length()-1:>9}"
              f" {(n.bit_length()-1)/2:>11.1f} {hi.bit_length()-1:>9}")
    print("\n   In min-plus coordinates the hyperbola xy = N is a line whose corner")
    print("   sits at sqrt(N); the noise floor 2/sqrt(N) is that corner.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# main
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    small_pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(3, 5), (3, 7), (5, 7), (5, 11), (7, 11), (11, 13)]
    big_pairs: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [
        (3, 65537), (101, 103), (1009, 1013), (10007, 10009), (65521, 65537)
    ]

    demo_agreement(small_pairs)
    demo_flipping_unit(5, 7)
    demo_zero_divisor_graph(5, 7)
    demo_zero_divisor_graph(7, 11)
    demo_noise_floor(small_pairs + big_pairs)
    demo_rho_collision(11, 13)
    demo_rho_collision(23, 29)
    demo_digit_lattice(10, [(11, 13), (23, 29), (37, 41), (59, 97)])
    demo_digit_lattice(16, [(19, 23), (101, 103), (211, 251)])
    demo_tropical_corner(small_pairs + big_pairs)

    print("=" * 74)
    print("All assertions passed: every closure verified on explicit numbers.")
    print("=" * 74)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.description: A comparative study across a family of balanced semiprimes that makes the scoping of the noise-floor principle quantitative. For each N = pq it reports the atomic uniform success density (p+q-2)/N alongside the balanced floor 2/sqrt(N), the index at which the rho walk first collides modulo p (compared with the birthday scale sqrt(p) and the pigeonhole guarantee p), the number of pairwise gcds an exhaustive aggregation spends before it succeeds, and the number of steps Floyd cycle detection needs. The table shows the correlated sample set is genuinely dense while unstructured aggregation is quadratic in the window, so only cycle detection plus the birthday heuristic - a known method - reaches the sqrt(p) regime.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Scaling study: what the correlated rho sampler actually buys.

For a family of balanced semiprimes N = p*q we compare, on explicit numbers:

  * the success density of ONE atomic uniform query,  delta(N) = (p+q-2)/N,
    against the balanced noise floor 2/sqrt(N) and the cap 2/min(p,q);

  * the first index at which the rho walk x -> x^2 + 1 collides modulo p
    (guaranteed by pigeonhole to occur by index p, with no randomness), and
    the empirical collision index, which behaves like sqrt(p) -- the birthday
    scale;

  * the number of pairwise gcds that unstructured aggregation actually spends
    before returning a factor, compared with the p trial divisions it was
    trying to beat.

The output makes the scoping statement concrete: the correlated sample set is
dense (a collision is certain), but converting the density into a factor by
pairwise comparison is never cheaper than trial division. Only cycle detection
plus the birthday heuristic -- a known method -- reaches the sqrt(p) regime.

Standard library only.  Run:  python3 demo2.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from math import gcd, sqrt
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


def rho_orbit(x0: int, n: int, steps: int) -> List[int]:
    orbit = [x0 % n]
    for _ in range(steps):
        orbit.append((orbit[-1] * orbit[-1] + 1) % n)
    return orbit


def first_collision_mod(orbit: List[int], p: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """The first pair of indices whose iterates agree modulo p."""
    seen: dict = {}
    for t, x in enumerate(orbit):
        r = x % p
        if r in seen:
            return (seen[r], t)
        seen[r] = t
    return None


def pairwise_extract(orbit: List[int], n: int) -> Tuple[Optional[int], int]:
    """Exhaustive pairwise gcds; returns (factor or None, gcds performed)."""
    performed = 0
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(orbit)), 2):
        performed += 1
        g = gcd(abs(orbit[j] - orbit[i]), n)
        if 1 < g < n:
            return g, performed
    return None, performed


def floyd_extract(x0: int, n: int, limit: int) -> Tuple[Optional[int], int]:
    """Floyd cycle detection: one gcd per step, the known-method shortcut."""
    tortoise = hare = x0 % n
    for step in range(1, limit + 1):
        tortoise = (tortoise * tortoise + 1) % n
        hare = (hare * hare + 1) % n
        hare = (hare * hare + 1) % n
        g = gcd(abs(hare - tortoise), n)
        if 1 < g < n:
            return g, step
        if g == n:
            return None, step
    return None, limit


def main() -> None:
    families: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [
        (11, 13), (23, 29), (101, 103), (211, 223), (503, 509),
        (1009, 1013), (2003, 2011), (5003, 5009),
    ]
    header = (f"{'p':>6} {'q':>6} {'N':>11} {'delta(N)':>11} {'2/sqrt(N)':>11} "
              f"{'collide@':>9} {'~sqrt(p)':>9} {'pair gcds':>10} {'Floyd':>7} {'trial p':>8}")
    print("=" * len(header))
    print("CORRELATED SAMPLER: density is free, aggregation is not")
    print("=" * len(header))
    print(header)
    for p, q in families:
        n = p * q
        delta = (p + q - 2) / n
        floor = 2 / sqrt(n)
        window = min(p + 1, 4000)
        orbit = rho_orbit(2, n, window)
        coll = first_collision_mod(orbit, p)
        assert coll is not None, "pigeonhole guarantees a collision by index p"
        assert coll[1] <= p
        factor, gcds = pairwise_extract(orbit[:min(len(orbit), 600)], n)
        fl_factor, fl_steps = floyd_extract(2, n, 4000)
        assert delta <= 2 / min(p, q)
        assert (p + q) ** 2 >= 4 * n
        print(f"{p:>6} {q:>6} {n:>11} {delta:>11.3e} {floor:>11.3e} "
              f"{coll[1]:>9} {sqrt(p):>9.1f} {gcds:>10} {fl_steps:>7} {p:>8}")
    print()
    print("Reading the table:")
    print("  * delta(N) hugs the balanced floor 2/sqrt(N): blind guessing is hopeless.")
    print("  * the rho walk collides at about sqrt(p) -- far earlier than the")
    print("    pigeonhole guarantee at p -- so the sample set really is dense.")
    print("  * 'pair gcds' counts what an exhaustive pairwise scan spends before it")
    print("    stumbles on a good pair; its worst case is C(T,2), quadratic in the window")
    print("    T, and the unconditional guarantee only holds at T = p+1, i.e. >= p gcds.")
    print("  * only Floyd cycle detection, one gcd per step, reaches the sqrt(p) regime,")
    print("    and that is the recognised known-method exception, not a new escape.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Jacobi-Symbol Evaluation of the Legendre Agreement Predicate
algorithms.description: Decides membership in the agreement set A(N) = {a : (a|p) = (a|q)} using only N, by evaluating the Jacobi symbol J(a|N) with the reciprocity-driven Euclidean algorithm. The mathematical foundation is that both Legendre symbols take values in {+1,-1}, so they are equal exactly when their product - which is precisely the Jacobi symbol - equals +1. The routine also computes the aggregate count and compares it with phi(N)/2, and exhibits the flipping unit u (a non-residue mod p, a square mod q) whose translation action carries A(N) bijectively onto its complement and thereby forces the count. Complexity: O(log^2 N) bit operations per membership test; the count check is O(N log^2 N) and is intended for verification on small semiprimes. Role in the pipeline: it demonstrates that the both-symmetries-invariant aggregate is N-computable, hence carries no information about the factors.

algorithms.name: Wing Decomposition and Degree Analysis of the Zero-Divisor Graph
algorithms.description: Computes the complete structure of the zero-divisor graph of Z/pqZ and reads the factorization off it in three independent ways: from the two wing sizes q-1 and p-1; from any single vertex degree, since degree plus one is always a prime factor; and from the vertex count p+q-2, whose increment by two is the trace s = p+q of the quadratic X^2 - sX + N with roots p and q. The routine also verifies the complete bipartite adjacency law (an edge exists exactly between opposite wings) and exhibits the circularity: the gcd of the very first vertex with N is already a nontrivial factor. Complexity: the wing enumeration is O(p+q) and the adjacency verification is O((p+q)^2) multiplications, i.e. linear and quadratic in the vertex count, which is itself the trial-division scale - precisely the aggregation cost that seals the structural witness.

function ANALYZE_ZDG(p, q):
    N <- p*q
    W_p <- { p, 2p, ..., (q-1)p }        # |W_p| = q-1
    W_q <- { q, 2q, ..., (p-1)q }        # |W_q| = p-1
    V   <- W_p union W_q                  # |V| = p+q-2, wings disjoint
    for x in V:  deg(x) <- |W_q| if p divides x else |W_p|
    assert for all x != y in V:
        (N divides x*y)  <=>  (x, y lie in opposite wings)
    assert for all x in V: (deg(x)+1) divides N
    s <- |V| + 2                          # the trace p+q
    d <- isqrt(s*s - 4N)
    return roots ((s-d)/2, (s+d)/2), and gcd(first vertex, N)

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def zero_divisor_wings(n: int, divisor: int) -> List[int]:
    """The wing of a divisor d of n: the nonzero multiples of d below n."""
    return list(range(divisor, n, divisor))


def analyze_zero_divisor_graph(p: int, q: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Compute the full structure of the zero-divisor graph of Z/pqZ and read the
    factorization off it in three independent ways:
      (a) the wing sizes,           (b) any single vertex degree,
      (c) the vertex count as the trace p + q of X^2 - sX + N.
    Returns a dictionary of the structural data together with the recovered pair.
    """
    n = p * q
    wing_p = zero_divisor_wings(n, p)
    wing_q = zero_divisor_wings(n, q)
    vertices = sorted(set(wing_p) | set(wing_q))
    degrees = {x: (len(wing_q) if x % p == 0 else len(wing_p)) for x in vertices}
    s = len(vertices) + 2
    disc = isqrt(s * s - 4 * n)
    roots = ((s - disc) // 2, (s + disc) // 2)
    sample = vertices[0]
    return {
        "N": n,
        "num_vertices": len(vertices),
        "wing_sizes": (len(wing_p), len(wing_q)),
        "is_complete_bipartite": all(
            ((x * y) % n == 0) == ((x % p == 0) != (y % p == 0))
            for i, x in enumerate(vertices) for y in vertices[i + 1:]
        ),
        "degree_plus_one_divides_N": all(n % (d + 1) == 0 for d in degrees.values()),
        "trace": s,
        "roots_from_trace": roots,
        "gcd_of_first_vertex": (sample, gcd(sample, n)),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for p, q in [(5, 7), (7, 11), (11, 13)]:
        for k, v in analyze_zero_divisor_graph(p, q).items():
            print(f"  {k:28s} {v}")
        print()

algorithms.description: Extracts a factor of N = pq from the correlated sample set of the static rho map x -> x^2 + 1 with no probabilistic assumption whatsoever. The foundation is twofold: the map commutes with reduction modulo any m, so the orbit mod N covers the orbit mod p; and the reduced orbit lives in only p states, so by pigeonhole two of the first p+1 iterates agree mod p. Any such collision that is not simultaneously a collision mod q satisfies gcd(x_j - x_i, N) = p exactly. Complexity: p+1 modular squarings for the orbit plus up to C(p+1,2) = Theta(p^2) gcd computations for the exhaustive pairwise scan - already above the p trial divisions the method sought to avoid. This is the precise price of the sampler's density advantage, and the reason the noise-floor principle must be scoped to atomic uniform primitives rather than to derived correlated samples.
